title: 09 — Streaming Pipelines
html:
09 — Streaming Pipelines

The one idea: Structured Streaming lets you write a query as if over a static table, and Spark runs it repeatedly over the rows that have arrived since last time. The two things you must add that batch never needed are a checkpoint (so the query knows where it stopped) and, for anything stateful, a watermark (so it knows when it may forget).

1. The model: a stream is an unbounded table

---
title: Structured Streaming — unbounded input table, incremental query
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph IN["Input: unbounded table"]
        R1["rows at t1"]
        R2["rows at t2"]
        R3["rows at t3 ..."]
    end
    Q["Same DataFrame query<br/>run incrementally<br/>each trigger"]
    subgraph ST["State store<br/>(for aggregations, dedup, joins)"]
        S["partial aggregates<br/>seen keys"]
    end
    subgraph OUT["Result table"]
        O["rows written to sink<br/>according to output mode"]
    end
    CK[("Checkpoint<br/>offsets, commits, state")]
    IN --> Q --> OUT
    Q <--> ST
    Q <--> CK

Each trigger, Spark:

  1. Asks the source for new data since the last committed offsets.
  2. Writes the planned offset range to the checkpoint (write-ahead log).
  3. Runs the query on just that data, reading and updating state as needed.
  4. Writes results to the sink.
  5. Records the batch as committed in the checkpoint.

If the query crashes between steps 2 and 5, on restart it re-runs the same offset range. With a replayable source and an idempotent sink, the output is exactly-once.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders = (spark.readStream
          .table("prod.bronze.orders"))                 # Delta table as a streaming source

clean = (orders
         .filter(F.col("order_id").isNotNull())
         .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(18,2)")))

query = (clean.writeStream
         .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod/meta/checkpoints/orders_silver")
         .trigger(availableNow=True)
         .toTable("prod.silver.orders"))

query.awaitTermination()

2. Sources and sinks

Sources

Source Notes
Kafka format("kafka"); offsets per topic-partition; replayable within topic retention
Azure Event Hubs Use the Kafka source against the Event Hubs Kafka endpoint, or the Event Hubs connector
Auto Loader (cloudFiles) Incremental file ingestion with file tracking and schema evolution (see chapter 07)
Delta table readStream.table(...); reads new appends. Updates/deletes in the source table fail the stream unless you set skipChangeCommits or read the Change Data Feed
Rate / memory Testing only 
kafka_df = (spark.readStream
    .format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker1:9092,broker2:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "orders")
    .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
    .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 500000)      # rate limit per micro-batch
    .load())

schema = "order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, amount DOUBLE, event_time TIMESTAMP"

orders = (kafka_df
    .select(F.col("key").cast("string").alias("kafka_key"),
            F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("o"),
            "topic", "partition", "offset", F.col("timestamp").alias("kafka_ts"))
    .select("kafka_key", "o.*", "topic", "partition", "offset", "kafka_ts"))

Keep topic, partition and offset in bronze: together they uniquely identify a message and make deduplication and debugging easy.

For Event Hubs via the Kafka endpoint, the bootstrap server is <namespace>.servicebus.windows.net:9093 with SASL_SSL; authenticate with Entra ID (OAuth) or a connection string stored in a secret scope, never hard-coded.

Sinks

Sink Exactly-once? Notes
Delta table Yes Transactional commits keyed by batch ID
Kafka At-least-once Downstream consumers should deduplicate
foreachBatch Depends on your code Make the batch function idempotent (§9)
foreach Depends on your code Row-at-a-time custom writer; rarely the best choice
Console / memory n/a Debugging

3. Triggers

Trigger Behaviour Use when
(default, none set) Next micro-batch starts as soon as the previous finishes Lowest latency with micro-batches; always-on compute
processingTime="1 minute" Micro-batch at a fixed interval Continuous jobs where a steady cadence is fine
availableNow=True Process everything available now, in possibly several batches respecting rate limits, then stop Scheduled incremental jobs; batch-like cost with streaming bookkeeping
once=True Old version of availableNow that processed everything in one batch; deprecated Replace with availableNow
continuous="1 second" Experimental low-latency mode with limited operator support Rarely; check current support before relying on it

availableNow is the most under-appreciated tool here. A job running every 15 minutes with availableNow gets exactly-once incremental processing, checkpoints and schema handling, but pays for compute only while it runs.

4. Checkpoints

The checkpoint directory holds:

Item Purpose
offsets/ Write-ahead log: which source offsets each batch will process
commits/ Which batches finished
state/ State store files for stateful operators
metadata Query ID
sources/ Source-specific tracking (e.g. files seen)

Rules:

  • One checkpoint per query, forever. Never share a checkpoint between two queries.
  • Store it in durable storage (a UC volume or cloud path), not on the driver's local disk.
  • Changing the query can break the checkpoint. Adding a filter or a stateless projection is usually fine; changing aggregation keys, adding or removing stateful operators, or changing the source is not. Treat such changes as a new query: new checkpoint, and decide how to backfill.
  • Deleting the checkpoint means the query starts from scratch (from startingOffsets or the beginning of the Delta table), which can duplicate output.

5. Output modes

Mode Writes each trigger Allowed with Typical sink
Append Only new rows that will never change Stateless queries; aggregations with a watermark (row emitted once its window closes) Delta, Kafka, files
Update Rows that changed since the last trigger Aggregations; sink must handle upserts foreachBatch + MERGE
Complete The entire result table Aggregations only; state never shrinks Small summary tables, dashboards

For a windowed aggregation into a Delta table, append mode with a watermark is the usual choice: each window's row is written once, after the watermark passes the window end. The cost is latency — results appear only when the window is finalised.

6. Event time, watermarks and late data

Events carry an event time; they arrive at the pipeline at processing time. Network delays, retries and offline mobile devices mean events arrive out of order and late.

A watermark tells Spark how late data is allowed to be:

watermark = max(event_time seen so far) − allowed delay
  • Windows ending before the watermark are finalised: emitted (in append mode) and their state dropped.
  • Events older than the watermark may be dropped — Spark guarantees to include data that is within the delay, but data beyond it is not guaranteed either way.
---
title: Watermark with a 10-minute allowed delay
---
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Stream
    participant E as Engine
    S->>E: event_time 12:14 arrives
    E->>E: max seen 12:14, watermark 12:04
    S->>E: event_time 12:07 arrives (late but within 10 min)
    E->>E: counted in window 12:05 to 12:10
    S->>E: event_time 12:21 arrives
    E->>E: watermark 12:11, window 12:05 to 12:10 finalised and emitted
    S->>E: event_time 12:08 arrives (older than watermark)
    E->>E: dropped, its window is already closed

Choosing the delay is a business trade-off: longer delay = more complete results, more state, higher latency. Measure the actual lateness distribution of your data (e.g. processing_time - event_time percentiles) and choose a delay that covers, say, p99.9. For data later than that, run a periodic batch correction from bronze rather than extending the watermark indefinitely.

7. Window types in code

events = (spark.readStream.table("prod.bronze.clicks")
          .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes"))

# Tumbling: 5-minute non-overlapping windows
tumbling = events.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "page").count()

# Sliding: 10-minute windows every 2 minutes
sliding = events.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes", "2 minutes"), "page").count()

# Session: per user, closes after 30 minutes of inactivity
sessions = (events
    .groupBy(F.session_window("event_time", "30 minutes"), "user_id")
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("clicks"),
         F.min("event_time").alias("session_start"),
         F.max("event_time").alias("session_end")))

(tumbling
    .select(F.col("window.start").alias("window_start"),
            F.col("window.end").alias("window_end"), "page", "count")
    .writeStream
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod/meta/checkpoints/page_counts_5m")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
    .toTable("prod.gold.page_counts_5m"))

8. Stateful operations and state stores

Operation State kept How state is cleaned up
Windowed aggregation Partial aggregates per (window, key) Watermark passes window end
Non-windowed aggregation (groupBy("user_id").count()) One entry per key, forever Never — avoid on unbounded key spaces, or use arbitrary stateful processing with timeouts/TTL
dropDuplicates / dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark Seen keys Watermark (include the event-time column, or use dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark)
Stream-stream join Buffered rows from both sides Watermarks on both sides plus an event-time range condition in the join
Arbitrary stateful processing (applyInPandasWithState, transformWithState on newer runtimes) Whatever you store Timeouts / TTL you define 
# Deduplicate on event_id, tolerating duplicates that arrive up to 1 hour apart
deduped = (spark.readStream.table("prod.bronze.events")
           .withWatermark("event_time", "1 hour")
           .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))

# Stream-stream join: impressions and clicks within 30 minutes
impressions = spark.readStream.table("prod.bronze.impressions").withWatermark("imp_time", "1 hour")
clicks      = spark.readStream.table("prod.bronze.clicks").withWatermark("click_time", "1 hour")

attributed = impressions.join(
    clicks,
    F.expr("""
        click_ad_id = imp_ad_id AND
        click_time >= imp_time AND
        click_time <= imp_time + interval 30 minutes
    """),
    "leftOuter")

State store backends: the default keeps state in executor JVM memory (with snapshots to the checkpoint), which hurts with large state because of GC. The RocksDB state store keeps state on local disk with an in-memory cache and scales to much larger state; Databricks recommends it for large stateful workloads.

spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")

Set this before the query first starts; the provider is recorded in the checkpoint.

9. foreachBatch with MERGE

Streaming writes to Delta are appends. To upsert a stream (CDC, latest-state tables), use foreachBatch, which gives you each micro-batch as a regular DataFrame.

from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

def upsert_customers(batch_df, batch_id):
    # 1. Deduplicate within the micro-batch: keep the latest change per key
    w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("change_ts").desc())
    latest = (batch_df
              .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
              .filter("rn = 1")
              .drop("rn"))

    target = DeltaTable.forName(batch_df.sparkSession, "prod.silver.customers")

    # 2. Merge, ignoring changes older than what we already have (out-of-order safety)
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
        .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'DELETE' AND s.change_ts >= t.change_ts")
        .whenMatchedUpdate(
            condition="s.op <> 'DELETE' AND s.change_ts > t.change_ts",
            set={"name": "s.name", "email": "s.email", "city": "s.city",
                 "change_ts": "s.change_ts"})
        .whenNotMatchedInsert(
            condition="s.op <> 'DELETE'",
            values={"customer_id": "s.customer_id", "name": "s.name", "email": "s.email",
                    "city": "s.city", "change_ts": "s.change_ts"})
        .execute())

(spark.readStream.table("prod.bronze.customers_cdc")
    .writeStream
    .foreachBatch(upsert_customers)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod/meta/checkpoints/customers_silver")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)
    .start())

Why this is exactly-once in effect: if a batch fails mid-way and is retried, the same batch is merged again, and because the merge is keyed and guarded by change_ts, applying it twice gives the same result.

If the batch function appends to Delta instead, make the write idempotent with the transaction options, so a retried batch is skipped:

def append_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    (batch_df.write.format("delta")
        .option("txnAppId", "orders_to_gold_v1")   # stable per query
        .option("txnVersion", batch_id)
        .mode("append")
        .saveAsTable("prod.gold.orders_flat"))

Other foreachBatch notes: writing the same batch to multiple sinks is allowed (cache the batch first if you read it several times); the batch function runs on the driver, but the DataFrame operations inside it are distributed as usual.

10. Monitoring streams

Signal Where Worry when
Input rows/sec vs processed rows/sec query.lastProgress, Spark UI Structured Streaming tab Processing rate stays below input rate: the stream is falling behind
Batch duration Same Longer than the trigger interval, or growing over time
Source lag (Kafka offsets behind latest, files backlog) Progress metrics (sources[].metrics), Kafka consumer lag tools Growing steadily
State rows and memory stateOperators in progress Growing without bound: missing or too-long watermark
Watermark value eventTime.watermark in progress Stuck: one partition has no new data, or event times are bad
Failures / restarts Job run history, alerts Any unexplained restart 
from pyspark.sql.streaming import StreamingQueryListener

class ProgressLogger(StreamingQueryListener):
    def onQueryStarted(self, event):
        print(f"started {event.id}")

    def onQueryProgress(self, event):
        p = event.progress
        print(p.name, p.batchId, p.numInputRows, p.inputRowsPerSecond, p.processedRowsPerSecond)

    def onQueryIdle(self, event):
        pass

    def onQueryTerminated(self, event):
        print(f"terminated {event.id}, exception={event.exception}")

spark.streams.addListener(ProgressLogger())

In production, send these metrics to your monitoring system instead of printing, and alert on lag and on batch duration.

11. Streaming design checklist in practice

Decision Default choice
Trigger availableNow on a schedule unless latency requirements demand always-on
Checkpoint One per query in a UC volume, named after the query and a version suffix
Bronze Append raw with source metadata (offsets, file path, ingestion time)
Silver foreachBatch MERGE for entities; append with dedup for events
Stateful ops Always with a watermark; RocksDB state store for large state
Late data beyond watermark Periodic batch correction from bronze
Schema changes Evolve in bronze, enforce in silver
Rate limiting maxOffsetsPerTrigger / maxFilesPerTrigger / maxBytesPerTrigger to keep batches predictable

Azure / .NET mapping

Concept Azure / .NET
Event source Azure Event Hubs (Kafka endpoint), Event Hubs Capture to ADLS for cheap raw landing
Producing events from .NET Azure.Messaging.EventHubs.Producer.EventHubProducerClient, or Confluent.Kafka against the Kafka endpoint
Alternative stream processors Azure Stream Analytics (SQL-like, managed), Fabric Real-Time Intelligence
Secrets for connection strings Key Vault-backed secret scope, or Entra ID OAuth for Event Hubs
Monitoring Stream metrics forwarded to Azure Monitor / Log Analytics

If you produce events from a .NET service, include a stable event ID and an event timestamp set at the source. Those two fields make deduplication and event-time processing possible downstream; without them, the pipeline has to guess.

Review checklist

  • I can explain the unbounded-table model and what happens in each trigger.
  • I know what the checkpoint stores and which query changes break it.
  • I can choose between default, processingTime and availableNow triggers.
  • I know which output modes are valid for which queries.
  • I can explain how a watermark is computed and what happens to data older than it.
  • Every stateful operation in my streams has a watermark or TTL.
  • I can write a foreachBatch MERGE that is safe to retry and robust to out-of-order changes.
  • I know how to make foreachBatch appends idempotent with txnAppId / txnVersion.
  • I monitor input vs processing rate, lag and state size.
